newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Fischler says EU will not undercut U.S. wheat.
newsitem.headline: Fischler says EU will not undercut U.S. wheat.

text.p: European Union Farm Commissioner Franz Fischler early on Friday defended EU export subsidies for wheat and vowed the EU would refrain from undercutting American wheat on the international market.
Speaking to Reuters after a grain industry dinner in Belgium, Fischler sought to calm U.S. concerns that recently restored EU subsidies could distort world wheat prices.

"We are not spending excessive subsidies. We are spending for the difference with international prices, and our basis is more or less the Chicago exchange so therefore I think there is no distortion on the market between the U.S. and Europe."
Asked whether the EU planned to undercut U.S. export prices that are driven by Chicago futures, Fischler said, "No."
The pledge to keep in step with U.S. prices echoed recent remarks by EU director-general for agriculture Guy Legras.
The EU, ending a year-long subsidy truce between Washington and Europe for wheat sales, resumed subsidised exports last month in the face of increasingly strident U.S. warnings.
U.S. Agrictulture Secretary Dan Glickman said last week that Washington stood ready to fight subsidies with subsidies if necessary to protect U.S. grain production.
"If, in fact, we see a serious and appreciable interest by the Europeans to weave their subsidised tentacles throughout the world, then we will take action," he said.
Fischler said EU actions were in line with the commitments negotiated between Washington and the EU in the Uruguay Round. These allowed subsidised exports up to agreed ceilings.
"I must say that at this stage what we are doing is completely in line with our WTO (World Trde Organisation) rules and we have no interest in going further," he said.
Fischler said he had replied in similar terms to a letter he had received recently from Glickman on the subsidy issue.

"What I can promise the Americans is that we are in line, and we will be in line, with our obligations of the Uruguay Round, and if we fulfill all our obligations there is no reason why we can't also use our possibilities," he said.
The WTO agreement, which took effect last year, sets a ceiling on subsidised grain export volumes and spending. Both must then be reduced in stages up to the year 2001.
But subsidies were not needed during the first year of the accord when grain markets were suddenly tight.
Grain analysts have said the U.S. may not need to restore wheat subsidies any time soon as stocks there remain low.

For its part, the EU may hope to avoid a direct clash with Washington as poor crops in eastern Europe provide a ready local market for its wheat, traders at the Antwerp gathering said. Less subsidy is needed for nearby destinations.

On Thursday, the EU granted wheat export subsidies of up to six Ecus per tonne. Traders said these equated to an export price of some $171 per tonne, which was slightly higher than the current prices for unsubsidised U.S. soft red winter wheat.
